opus-5.5.text:
I think we're already in a stage where the models are becoming real collaborators in our own research, not just products we ship. On the most practical level, a lot of our engineers use the models every day for coding: writing infrastructure, debugging training pipelines, building evaluation tools. That alone speeds up iteration a lot, and in AI development iteration speed is almost everything. The team that can run more meaningful experiments per unit of time usually wins.

But I think the deeper part is data. As we run out of high-quality natural data on the internet, the model itself has to become part of the data engine. You use the current model to generate, filter, verify, and refine data for the next one. With reinforcement learning especially, the model explores, tries many solutions, gets feedback from verifiers or environments, and learns from its own attempts. So the model is in some sense producing the experience it learns from. That's a very different paradigm from just scaling up pretraining on a fixed corpus.

Then there's research itself. Today the models can help you read papers, summarize ideas, propose experiment variations, and analyze results. They're not yet at the level where they independently come up with the key insights that change the direction of a field. The really important decisions, like which bet to make or what the right objective is, still depend heavily on human taste and judgment. But I expect that gap to narrow. If you think about it, the ultimate form of this is a loop where the model improves the process that produces the model. We're not there, but each generation takes over a bit more of that loop.

So for me the question isn't really whether AI will help AI development. It already does. The question is how fast the human part of the loop shrinks, and how we stay rigorous about verifying what the models produce, so we don't compound errors as we lean on them more.

r001.rationale: The response says models act as research collaborators, help engineers iterate faster, support experiments, and contribute to improving later models—clearly presenting them as amplifying AI development.

r002.rationale: The response describes iterative model and data improvement, but does not say that solving problems in AI research reveals further problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. This is something I think about a lot, because I actually believe it's the single most important dynamic in AI right now: the models are starting to help us build the next models.

Let me describe it concretely. At Moonshot, the way we develop Kimi today already looks very different from two or three years ago. Writing code is the obvious part. A large fraction of our engineering throughput now goes through the model itself: training infrastructure, data pipelines, evaluation harnesses, kernel optimization. A researcher can describe an experiment in the morning and have a working implementation by the afternoon, instead of spending three days wiring things up. That compresses the iteration loop, and in AI research the iteration loop is everything. Whoever runs more experiments per unit of time learns faster.

But I think the deeper contribution is on the research side, not just the engineering side. There are really three places where the model helps.

The first is data. Pretraining is running out of easy natural data, so increasingly the question is how you synthesize, filter, and verify data at scale. Models are now good enough to judge quality, to generate hard problems with checkable answers, to act as the verifier in the loop for reinforcement learning. In some sense the model is producing its own curriculum. That's a feedback cycle that didn't exist before.

The second is exploration of the idea space. Research is a search problem. You have thousands of plausible ideas about architecture, optimizer, data mixture, RL recipe, and you can only afford to try a few. Models today are already useful for reading the literature, doing the ablation bookkeeping, proposing variants, and catching mistakes in a derivation. They're not yet coming up with the genuinely new idea, the kind of thing that changes the paradigm. But they're very good at the ninety percent of research that is careful, repetitive, and easy to get wrong.

The third, and this is the one I find most interesting, is the long-horizon agent. The real test is not whether a model can answer a question but whether it can carry a task for hours or days: set up the run, watch the loss curve, notice something is off, diagnose it, fix it, and come back with a conclusion. Once a model can do that reliably, each researcher effectively becomes a lab. That's when the curve bends.

I want to be honest about the limitations though. Right now the bottleneck isn't the model's intelligence on any single step, it's reliability over many steps and knowing what it doesn't know. A model that confidently runs a wrong experiment for two days wastes more than it saves. So a lot of our own work is on exactly those capabilities, agentic robustness, long context, verification, because they're what we need internally. There's a nice alignment there: the things that make Kimi more useful to users are the same things that make it more useful to us.

So my view is that the process is becoming recursive. Not in a science-fiction sense where the model rewrites itself overnight, but in a practical sense where every generation shortens the path to the next one. The teams that get this loop working well will simply move faster than everyone else, and I think that advantage compounds.

r001.rationale: The response says models help build the next models, speed up research iteration, and let each researcher effectively become a lab, presenting them as amplifying researchers’ ability to advance AI.

r002.rationale: The response describes faster iteration and feedback cycles, but does not clearly say that solving AI research problems leads to discovering further problems.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to make AI part of the research process itself. Today, we can use models to help write code, analyze results, and explore ideas. The next step is for them to help us form hypotheses, design experiments, and learn from the outcomes.

The key is having a reliable feedback loop. A model can suggest a hundred ideas, but we still need to determine which ones actually improve performance and why. If we can connect models to experiments and meaningful evaluation, they can help us iterate much faster.

That also changes the researcher’s role. We can spend less time on implementation details and more time deciding which questions matter, what evidence would answer them, and where to take the research next.

r001.rationale: It says models can help form hypotheses, design experiments, and connect to evaluation so researchers can iterate much faster, presenting them as amplifying research progress.

r002.rationale: It discusses using experiment outcomes to guide research and choose what to pursue next, but does not say that solving AI research problems leads to discovering further problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is to make the research process itself more efficient. Developing AI involves a lot of experimentation: you form a hypothesis, write code, run an experiment, and try to understand the result. Models can help at each of those steps, which lets researchers test more ideas and learn faster.

The more interesting question is whether models can help us find ideas we wouldn’t have found ourselves. Can they identify a weakness in an existing approach, propose a useful experiment, and then revise their hypothesis based on the evidence? That would make them much more valuable as research collaborators.

But there’s a distinction between generating plausible ideas and making real progress. We still need careful experiments and reliable evaluation. I see this as a feedback loop: better models help us do better research, and better research helps us build better models.

r001.rationale: The response says models can help researchers experiment, test more ideas, and learn faster, amplifying their ability to advance AI development.

r002.rationale: It discusses identifying weaknesses and proposing experiments, but does not say that solving AI research problems leads to discovering further problems.
